name: intx (fixed-size 256/512-bit integers)
baseline: GMP (low-level mpn_tdiv_qr and mpn_mul_n, called through the repo's own wrappers in test/utils/gmp.hpp)
workload: The repo's intx-bench (Google Benchmark, test/benchmarks/benchmarks.cpp) times uint256 and uint512 udivrem against gmp::udivrem (mpn_tdiv_qr) for divisors of 64, 128, 192 and 256 bits, and uint256 and uint512 multiplication against gmp::mul and gmp::mul_full (mpn_mul_n).
claimed_speedup: None published. The benchmark harness that pits intx against GMP exists, but no result, ratio or table is committed or quoted in the README, CHANGELOG, the PRs and issues I opened (#99, #129, #147, #194, #267, #55, #291, #367) or any other page I could open. The only numbers on those pages compare intx with earlier intx (for example PR #99: 256-bit division about 40% faster, 512-bit about 10% slower, 'Time Old/New' 55146 -> 33118 for uint256/uint64).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for any GMP comparison. Build per README: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default for GCC/Clang Release is -O3 -DNDEBUG); intx-bench adds -falign-functions=32 on GCC/Clang (test/benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt); no -march flag there.
stars_or_usage: 176 stars, 41 forks (github.com page); the task lead says it is used by Ethereum clients, which I could not confirm on an opened page (the ethereum/aleth issue 5720 only proposes replacing boost::multiprecision with intx and has no numbers).
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, allocation-free fixed-width types stored as arrays of uint64_t words (uint128, uint256, uint384, uint512 and any word count); no variable-size integers, so it is not a replacement for GMP mpz. Behaves like built-in unsigned types; division and modular helpers (addmod, mulmod, exp) target EVM and elliptic-curve use.
caveats: Does not qualify as a speed claim yet: no published number against GMP, so tier D. The code to measure it is public (Apache-2.0, GMP linked via find_package(GMP)), so a later pass could run intx-bench and promote it. Counter-evidence for 128-bit: in a third-party harness (https://github.com/mikelik/int128-benchmark, README, GCC run, 20-core CPU at 4600 MHz, flags and CPU model not stated) intx::uint128 is slower than boost::multiprecision::uint128_t: add 16.8 ns vs 13.2 ns, multiply 15.2 ns vs 13.1 ns; that repo has no GMP benchmark. The repo's README, CHANGELOG (0.15.0 dated 2026-01-30) and docs carry no performance table; docs/benchmarks.md returned 404. WebSearch (1 query) found no published intx-vs-GMP numbers.

name: ECM-ELF (ECM stage 1, AVX-512 IFMA 8-curve batch backend)
language: C/C++ (GitHub lists C as primary; the AVX-512 kernels are .cpp; CUDA and OpenCL backends also exist)
baseline: GMP-ECM 7.0.6 (ecm-zen3.exe, built on GMP, curve family -param 0); the same table also compares Prime95 v31.04b05 (GWNUM FFT)
workload: Elliptic-curve-method stage 1 only (B2=0 or B2=B1), Suyama sigma Montgomery curves, one thread on one physical core, on Mersenne numbers 2^k-1 (M127 to M19701), per-curve seconds; the SIMD backend runs 8 curves per batch (time divided by 8). Directly measured case: N = M4001 = 2^4001-1 at B1 = 1e5, 1e6 and 2e6.
claimed_speedup: docs/ECM_Montgomery_STAGE1.md section 14.2, M4001, per curve: B1=1e5 0.596 s vs GMP-ECM 1.787 s (3.00x faster); B1=1e6 6.264 s vs 15.008 s (2.40x faster); B1=2e6 13.455 s vs about 30 s (scaled, about 2.2x). Section 14.5 size sweep at B1=1e6: M1277 0.979 s vs 2.484 s (2.54x), M2203 2.285 s vs 5.804 s (2.54x), M3001 4.137 s vs 9.586 s (2.32x), M3500 5.164 s vs 11.656 s (2.26x), M4001 6.290 s vs 14.624 s (2.32x); about 1.7x (fitted) at M5755 and M8527. Against Prime95: 32.7x at M127, 10.4x at M521, 3.94x at M1277 but 0.90x at M4001 and 0.17x at M19701 (fitted); the doc says the new code is worthwhile below about 3700 bits and Prime95's FFT is the better choice above about 6000 bits, with mixed results in between. Section 10.4 (earlier, before clocks were pinned), M1277 B1=1e6: 1.418 s vs 3.551 s per curve (2.50x).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC Release build (build_vs18\Release\ecm.exe, MSVC /O2 per README); the two AVX-512 translation units src/cpu/simd_mont_ifma.cpp and simd_edwards.cpp get /arch:AVX512 (or -mavx512f -mavx512ifma -mavx512dq on GCC/Clang) in CMakeLists.txt. Commands are in section 14.1 and 14.4: echo (2^4001-1) | ecm.exe --mont --mont-backend simd --mont-threads 1 -gpucurves 8 --sigma 4242 <B1> 0, versus ecm-zen3.exe -param 0 -c 2 <B1> <B1>. The GMP-ECM baseline is a prebuilt multiarch Windows release (ecm-2025.10.28, --enable-asm-redc); its compiler and flags are not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 (Strix Point, Zen 5 plus Zen 5c, 256-bit FPU datapath so 512-bit IFMA runs as 2 x 256-bit); clocks pinned at 3990 MHz on the Zen 5 cores (logical CPUs 0-7) and 2995 MHz on Zen 5c; Windows (exe paths). Single-thread numbers stated reproducible to about +-3%.
tradeoffs: Stage 1 only (stage 2 is handed to Prime95 or GMP-ECM through compatible .save files). The fast path needs AVX-512 IFMA hardware (explicit error otherwise; auto falls back to a slow scalar mpn backend). Gains come from 8-lane batches, a Mersenne fold domain for N = 2^k-1 (about 2x faster than general N per the README) and affine differential ladder; general N uses Montgomery CIOS. Cost grows about n^1.66 in word count, so Prime95's FFT overtakes it above about 3700 bits. GPL-3.0 copyleft. Windows-first build; Chinese-language README (README.en.md exists). Renamed from OpenCL-ECM.
caveats: Strong methodology but one author, one laptop-class machine with hand-pinned clocks, mostly Mersenne inputs (special form), and a prebuilt third-party GMP-ECM binary without stated compile flags; the doc does not say whether GMP-ECM's special-form handling for 2^k-1 was active. Only the M4001 rows (section 14.2) and the section 10.4 rows are direct same-machine measurements; a footnote under the section 14.5 table says the own-implementation points for 1277 to 4001 bits use an extrapolation from the author's fit (about 2.98e-7*k^2 + 3.79e-4*k seconds) and its wording does not make clear which rows are direct measurements, M5755 and larger are fitted for all columns, and the Prime95 column is a FFT-length model calibrated on one measured M3001 point (5.65 s) plus the M4001 run at B1=1e7. The 'about 30 s' GMP-ECM figure at B1=2e6 is scaled, not measured. The doc itself notes Prime95 was running during the measurements and that the section 10.4 numbers predate clock pinning. The repo changes daily (the 2026-10-01 commits are on the GPU and stage 2 paths; one says a mathematically wrong optimisation was caught), and no bug in the CPU IFMA path turned up, but the numbers are dated 2026-09-24 and were not re-run against HEAD. The scalar GMP mpn backend of this repo is only a cross-check (about 5.6 s/curve at M1277, B1=1e5 versus 0.135 s/curve for SIMD in the same doc), so there is no win against raw GMP mpn arithmetic to claim. The GPU backends (CUDA CGBN, OpenCL) are compared with CGBN, not GMP, and are not covered here. Evidence-tier call (A) rests on public code, stated CPU, MSVC /O2 and /arch:AVX512, and exact commands; a verifier may lower it to C because the baseline binary's flags are unknown.

name: VROOM (RNS Montgomery arithmetic with AVX-512 IFMA, BLS12-381 and BN254)
baseline: BLST (supranational/blst at 8065152, a modified vendored copy in blst/ with benchmark wrappers); GMP is used only for parameter generation and validation, not timed
workload: Google Benchmark ns per operation for BLS12-381 field and curve operations (Fp mul, Fp2, Fp12, G1/G2 add, double, scalar multiplication, Miller loop, final exponentiation, full pairing), VROOM RNS code against BLST on the same machine; ratio = blst_ns / rns_ns.
claimed_speedup: results/bench_bls12_381_vs_blst.txt, MatrixNoK (the production configuration), VROOM ns vs BLST ns: full pairing 128145.9 vs 500035.1 (ratio 3.902); Miller loop 49888.2 vs 215023.1 (4.310); final exponentiation 82491.2 vs 285421.3 (3.460); Fp12 mul 257.1 vs 1563.4 (6.082); Fp12 sqr 224.4 vs 1126.2 (5.019); G1 add 154.2 vs 585.8 (3.799); G1 scalar mult (GLV) 30647.5 vs 75949.8 (2.478); G2 scalar mult (GLS) 41245.7 vs 146934.4 (3.562); Fp mul 21.8 vs 29.0 (1.332 for a single mul, up to 2.272 amortized in a batch of 10). The slower row: Fp12 inversion with the BLST inverter 7599.8 vs 5560.4 (0.732); the RNS-assisted inversion reaches 3406.7 (1.632). The plain Matrix variant gives pairing 151066.7 vs 500035.1 (3.310).
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 21.1.0 (LLVM 21 prebuilt, llvm-project 3623fe6) with Google Benchmark at 04ccbd8 (v1.9.4-89), --benchmark_min_time 0.5s (scripts/reproduce_cpu_bench.sh). VROOM benchmark: -std=c++20 -O3 -march=native -mavx512ifma -D__ADX__ (src/Makefile CXXFLAGS_BENCH). BLST baseline: blst/Makefile CFLAGS -O2 -fno-builtin -fPIC -D__x86_64__ (+ -D__ADX__ when /proc/cpuinfo shows adx), CC auto-detected as clang if present, field arithmetic from assembly_small.S.
hardware: AWS c7i.metal-24xl, Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C (Sapphire Rapids), Amazon Linux 2023 (kernel 6.1.x); raw JSON committed (results/bench_bls12_381.json, bench_blst_complete.json, run dated 2026-06-17, Google Benchmark reports 96 CPUs). Thread count of the benchmarks not stated; they look single-threaded.
stars_or_usage: 5 stars, 1 fork; research artifact (README refers to paper numbers, a camera-ready update and artifact evaluation)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX-512 IFMA hardware (a slow integer fallback exists for correctness only) and, per the README, clang 21.x for paper-comparable timings, because GCC and older clang are significantly slower on the IFMA path. Gains are largest on batched or compound operations (Fp12, pairing, scalar mult); a single Fp multiply is only 1.33x. Ships parameter sets for BLS12-381 and BN254 only; the MatrixNoK parameter search is exponential in the number of radix words, so it suits small moduli. README says: research-grade, not vetted or audited for security. The blst/ subtree stays Apache-2.0; baselines/ vendors arkworks, zkcrypto, zksync and gnark with their own licenses.
caveats: Tier capped at C under the project rule for numbers measured on code later fixed for correctness bugs: the committed results and the camera-ready README are from 2026-06-17, while commits of 2026-08-14 (2785394, 145f864) and 2026-08-28 (0131695) fixed the radix-to-RNS conversion (floor instead of ceiling, reported by an outside reviewer) and the MatrixNoK negative-input conversion; results/ was not touched afterwards. The commit diffs change precomputed constants and add a rounding mode, not operation counts, so a verifier may judge tier A defensible (public code, committed raw JSON, stated CPU, compiler and flags, artifact-evaluated). The same-machine pair is clean, but BLST is built at -O2 with assembly field arithmetic while VROOM uses -O3 -march=native; the pairing figure uses BLST's own inverter inside the RNS pairing (BM_Pairing_RNS_BLST_Inverter); amortized batch rows exclude any batching cost on the caller side; BLST is a modified vendored copy. The paper 'VROOM: Accelerating (Almost All) Number-Theoretic Cryptography' (IACR ePrint 2026/393) appeared in a WebSearch result but eprint.iacr.org was blocked by the egress proxy, so the paper's own numbers and venue were not opened. The task lead's baselines (GMP, MPFR) are not what this repo benchmarks against; BLST is the relevant incumbent for BLS12-381.

name: libQD3 (double-double, triple-double, quad-double, extended-double)
baseline: MPFR (the task lead also names original QD; the only numbers found put the upstream QD library against MPFR and GMP)
workload: No benchmark of libQD3 itself found. Indirect lead: MPLAPACK's Rgemm (dense matrix multiply) benchmark with the upstream QD library as the quad-double back end, against MPFR and GMP back ends, on one machine.
claimed_speedup: None in the libQD3 repo or its release notes. Indirect numbers from the MPLAPACK 2.0.1 manual (section 9, upstream QD, not libQD3): peak Rgemm reference versions quad-double 33 MFlops, GMP 19 MFlops, MPFR 11 MFlops; OpenMP versions quad-double 1.3 GFlops, GMP 693 MFlops, MPFR 390 MFlops (ratio to MPFR about 3.0x single-threaded and 3.3x OpenMP, derived from page data).
hardware: For the indirect MPLAPACK numbers: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X, 256 GB DDR4-3200 ECC, Docker, GCC 9.3.0 (flags not stated).
stars_or_usage: 2 stars, 0 forks; MPLAPACK (same author) now uses libQD3 as its QD back end per the MPLAPACK README
tradeoffs: Fixed-precision floating point built from 2 to 4 binary64 limbs (about 106, 159, 212 bits) or two binary80 limbs (EDD): binary64 exponent range, not correctly rounded, not arbitrary precision. Sloppy add, multiply and divide are on by default (a few bits of accuracy traded for speed); optional branch-free arithmetic (QD_ENABLE_BF*), FMA selection and x86-64-v3 or native code generation. C, C++ and Fortran interfaces. EDD needs binary80 long double (x87), with known MinGW/Wine trigonometry test failures.
caveats: Why tier D: libQD3's own text has no timing against MPFR or against original QD. What it has: docs/td.tex flop counts (for example TD add 41 flops vs QD 84, multiply 116/206 vs QD 182/332 with and without FMA, FMA speedup about 1.8x to 2.7x for multiplication, derived from counts rather than timings) and tests/qd_timer.cpp (a timer with no MPFR). The README says the fork 'keeps the original double-double and quad-double functionality' and adds TD, EDD, complex types, optional branch-free arithmetic, MPFR oracle tests; recent commits (2026-09-18) fix qd sqrt rescaling. The indirect MPLAPACK numbers (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nakatamaho/mplapack/master/doc/manual/manual.pdf, section 9, same author, arXiv 2109.13406 v2 of 2022) predate libQD3 (they used upstream QD), compare precisions that differ (quad-double about 212 bits against MPFR and GMP at their 512-bit default), go through MPLAPACK's C++ wrappers (the author suspects the MPFR wrapper copies needlessly because MPFR ran at half of GMP speed), and are not peer reviewed. Another web-search result title mentions a QD vs MPFR/GMP (212 bits) matrix-multiplication timing table of unknown authorship; it was not opened. A verifier may re-tier to C if it accepts the lineage argument. Benchmark data for the 2022 run sit in nakatamaho/mplapack benchmark/results/2022 (directory listing opened, files not read).

name: primefactors (CPU GMP/GMP-ECM reference plus CGBN GPU factoring programs)
baseline: GMP-ECM 7.0.6 (libecm, on GMP): the repo's own CPU reference path is GMP plus libecm, and the GPU programs are measured against it
workload: Prime factorization of semiprimes: Pollard's rho on GPU (CUDA with the author's CGBN fork) against CPU ECM on the same number, 16-digit factor; CPU ECM wall clock on a 32-core box for 30-, 35- and 40-digit factors.
claimed_speedup: None: the project claims no speedup and says the opposite. README 'Performance reality': the GPU programs 'do not beat the CPU for hard inputs'; for integers below 2^64 they are 'much slower than their GMP-ECM equivalent'; on an RTX 4080 a 16-digit factor takes about 8.7 s with GPU rho versus about 2 s for CPU ECM on the same number (about 4x slower, derived from page data), and 19-digit and larger factors are impractical. CPU path wall clock (32-core box, equal-size prime semiprime): 30-digit factor about 10.5 s, 35-digit about 20.6 s, 40-digit about 5.7 min.
compiler_and_flags: CPU: /usr/bin/gcc -O3 -std=c17 -funroll-loops -ftree-vectorize -ftree-slp-vectorize -fopenmp, link -lecm -lgmp -flto=32. GPU: nvcc (CUDA 12.9, also tested 13.2) -O3 -arch=sm_89 (sm_120 on Blackwell), OpenMPI 5.0.5, GMP-ECM 7.0.6 (all from the Makefile and README).
hardware: Tested on a laptop with RTX 4080 Ada (sm_89) and Core i9-14900HX, and an Intel NUC 13 Extreme with RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (sm_120) and Core i9-13900K, Fedora 41 and 44; the 32-core CPU box for the ECM timings is not identified.
tradeoffs: Hobby research code. primefactors.c is arbitrary precision through GMP mpz_t with trial division, Pollard's rho and GMP-ECM curves spread across cores by OpenMP (memory grows with threads times B1). The two CUDA programs (cgbnprimefactors.cu, ecmcgbnprimefactorsmpi.cu) need CUDA, the author's CGBN fork and OpenMPI; GPU rho gains only about sqrt(k) from k parallel walks. Single-machine ECM tops out around 45 digits per the README; MPI scaling was never tested beyond one node.
caveats: Does not qualify as faster than its baseline: the README and primefactors-design.pdf both state that neither GPU program is intended to beat the CPU GMP-ECM path, and the CPU path simply calls GMP and GMP-ECM, so no baseline is beaten. Kept as a record so the shortcoming is documented (not faster). The only comparison is first-party and has no methodology beyond the GPU model (8.7 s vs 2 s, one number). The ~37 s to ~8.65 s improvement in the design doc is GPU-against-GPU tuning. The README states the author used Claude Opus 5.0 for the Pollard's rho code and for testing and bug finding. Related: the author's CGBN fork (steleman/nvidia-cgbn) was not examined.
